pages.title: Three questions, one reading journey
pages.subtitle: R06 / AI Safety & Future Intelligence
sections: The question behind this research

What would let an AI do more than produce a convincing answer: understand a situation, anticipate consequences, choose an action, and remain under meaningful control? R06 approaches that question through three strands: world models, which represent and predict an environment; neurosymbolic systems, which combine learned patterns with explicit structure; and independent safety assessment, which examines evidence about capabilities and risks. These are connected questions, not one settled design.
Follow a single example

Imagine an assistant helping a robot put a cup on a shelf. It needs to recognize the cup, represent the shelf and obstacles, anticipate what different movements would do, and select an action. It must also recognize uncertainty and respect limits on what it may move. This is an illustrative teaching example, not a result reported by a source. Keep it in mind as the terminology becomes more technical.
What kind of evidence are you reading?

A position paper argues for a research direction. A survey organizes other work. An experiment tests a method under specified conditions, often using a benchmark, a repeatable task or test suite. A replication asks whether a result can be reproduced independently. The research compendium notes that R06 includes many proposals and blog posts. A compelling explanation therefore deserves a different level of confidence from repeated experimental evidence. [06.3, 06.5, 06.7, 06.11]
How to use this guide

Read the narrative first. Bold terms are explained where they appear; small vocabulary boxes reinforce distinctions used again later. The HTML companion and separate vocabulary PDF provide all 389 existing term-note entries grouped beside the corresponding learning topics. These are optional reference entries, not 389 claims newly verified for this guide. Listening prompts suggest where to pause when an idea arises in the podcast. For one primary reading, start with the DreamerV3 paper introduced on page 10. [06.5]
vocab: Capability
What a system can do under specified conditions.
Evidence
Observations or results that support a particular claim.
Hypothesis
A proposed explanation or mechanism that still needs testing.
pages.cue: When the podcast makes a broad claim about future intelligence, ask: is this a proposed architecture, a demonstrated result, or an interpretation?

pages.title: From observations to a world model
pages.subtitle: PART 1 / Representing the situation
sections: Keep what matters for the next decision

A world model is an internal model used to predict what might happen, including after a candidate action. A state describes the situation; a representation is the form in which the model encodes it. The robot does not necessarily need a perfect reconstruction of every pixel. It may need the cup position, shelf height, obstacles, and information about whether the cup is being held. Which details matter depends on the task. [06.3]
A representation is not automatically an understanding

A latent state is an internal, usually compressed representation rather than a directly observed measurement. An encoder converts observations into that representation. Compression alone does not guarantee that the model preserved the right physical relationships. A model may learn correlations that work in its training setting and fail when objects, lighting, or actions change. Ask what the representation enables, not whether the language used to describe it sounds human.
Two ways to predict

A generative model can produce observations such as images or video. A Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predicts a representation of a target rather than requiring a reconstruction of every detail. An embedding is a numerical representation in a learned space. In LeCun's proposed approach, prediction in representation space is meant to retain useful structure while leaving irrelevant detail aside. This is an architectural argument, not proof that every representation-space model captures causality. [06.3]
Make room for uncertainty

Aleatoric uncertainty concerns variability in the environment; epistemic uncertainty concerns gaps in the model's knowledge. A moving object may genuinely have several possible futures, or the model may simply lack information. Those situations call for different responses. A useful model should not disguise either one with a single confident-looking prediction.
vocab: Observation
A signal available to the system, such as a camera image.
Abstraction
A representation that keeps selected structure and leaves out detail.
Latent variable
An internal variable that can represent unobserved factors or alternative outcomes.
pages.cue: Pause at descriptions of a model that “understands the world.” What exactly is represented, what is predicted, and how would the claim be tested?

pages.title: Learning useful representations
pages.subtitle: PART 1 / Why prediction alone is not enough
sections: Where the learning signal comes from

Self-supervised learning (SSL) obtains a learning task from the data itself, for example predicting one part from another, rather than requiring a person to label every example. A model can observe how a scene changes and learn relationships between views or times. That is different from reinforcement learning, where behavior is improved using a reward or cost signal associated with actions. Observation and action can supply complementary information. [06.3]
The easy answer can be useless

An objective specifies what the learning procedure tries to improve; a loss expresses an error to reduce. If two encoders are rewarded only for producing matching representations, they could emit the same constant for everything. Their outputs would agree while distinguishing nothing. This is representation collapse. Good training must make predictions useful without allowing that shortcut.
Contrast and regularization

Contrastive learning distinguishes related examples from selected alternatives. Non-contrastive learning can instead use additional constraints to preserve informative representations. A regularizer discourages an undesirable or degenerate solution. VICReg, discussed in the existing notes, combines agreement with constraints on the spread of representation components and their correlations. Variance describes spread; covariance describes how components vary together. These are mechanisms for avoiding particular failures, not a universal guarantee of useful reasoning. [06.3]
Energy is a score here, not electricity

An energy-based model (EBM) assigns a compatibility score: compatible configurations receive low energy and incompatible ones higher energy. This use of “energy” is mathematical; it does not measure watts or carbon emissions. A gradient describes how a quantity changes locally with its inputs or parameters. Differentiability makes gradient-based optimization possible, but does not ensure that the objective represents what the user actually wants.
The founder's question

A learning curve can show that a numerical objective improved while leaving the practical question unanswered. Ask which information the representation must preserve, how collapse or shortcuts were ruled out, and whether the improvement transfers to the intended task. Separate the training objective from the outcome you care about.
vocab: Parameters
The adjustable values learned during training.
Inductive bias
A design preference that makes some solutions easier to learn than others.
VICReg
Variance-invariance-covariance regularization: a representation-learning criterion discussed in the notes.
pages.cue: When training is described as “learning without supervision,” distinguish learning without manual labels from learning without any objective or design choices.

pages.title: How a model becomes a plan
pages.subtitle: PART 1 / Predict, compare, act, then reconsider
sections: A prediction becomes useful when it changes a decision

A policy maps the available state or observation to an action. A planner considers alternatives before choosing one. In model-predictive control (MPC), the system predicts the consequences of candidate action sequences, scores them, executes the first action of a preferred sequence, and plans again using the updated situation. The planning horizon is how far ahead it considers. Replanning is also called receding-horizon control. [06.3]
The actor, the critic, and the objective

An actor proposes or selects actions. A critic estimates their value or future cost; it is a learned evaluator, not an independent human auditor. An action sequence is a candidate series of moves. A rollout is a sequence of predicted states under such moves. The planner can compare rollouts, but it remains limited by the model and by the scoring rule. Optimizing a poor objective can produce a very effective wrong answer.
Why longer plans can be difficult

Prediction mistakes can accumulate. Separately, when optimization differentiates through many repeated model steps, gradients can become extremely large or small: exploding or vanishing gradients. A local minimum is a nearby solution that looks better than its neighbors but need not be globally best. These are distinct difficulties. The existing notes caution that the podcast's “compounding error” explanation does not capture the specific gradient and optimization problems discussed in the GRASP post. [06.9]
Read GRASP as a specific proposal

The existing GRASP notes describe optimizing intermediate states alongside actions, adding noise to explore alternatives, and modifying gradient flow. Optimizing those intermediate states is called collocation or lifted-state planning. GRASP does not simply abandon states. Ask which failure it addresses, which experimental setting supports the result, and which assumptions remain. [06.9]
vocab: Cost function
A rule assigning a penalty to an outcome or trajectory.
Hierarchical planning
Planning through levels of goals and subgoals.
Feedback
New observations used to revise the next action.
pages.cue: Pause when a planner is called more intelligent or reliable. Identify its objective, horizon, feedback, and the conditions under which it was tested.

pages.title: Dreamer: learning through imagined experience
pages.subtitle: PART 1 / A worked example of model-based learning
sections: Keep the three components separate

DreamerV3 is described in the existing material as a model-based reinforcement-learning system: it learns a world model and uses predicted experience to improve behavior. The world model predicts outcomes; the actor chooses actions; the critic estimates value. “Imagination” here means computation over model states, not consciousness or human-like subjective experience. [06.5]
Real experience still anchors the system

A trajectory is a sequence of observations, actions, and outcomes. An experience replay buffer stores past trajectories so they can be reused during learning. The world model is trained from collected experience. The actor and critic can then learn from imagined rollouts inside it. Sample efficiency concerns how much real interaction is needed; it is different from computational efficiency, which concerns the processing needed to learn or act.
Why the reward matters

A reward scores outcomes for the learning task. A return combines rewards over a sequence, often giving less weight to distant rewards through discounting. The model, reward definition, and evaluation setting together shape the behavior that emerges. An impressive score can be meaningful without establishing that the same system will pursue the right goals in an unfamiliar deployment.
What the compiled result says

The research compendium reports performance across more than 150 tasks with one configuration. A hyperparameter is a setting chosen for the learning procedure rather than learned as a model parameter. Using one configuration across varied tasks is a robustness claim worth understanding. It is not proof of universal competence, safety, or transfer to arbitrary robots. The guide has not rechecked the original experiments. [06.5]
Read numbers with their denominators

Ask what counted as a task, a success, an episode, and a comparison baseline. An episode is one bounded interaction run. A baseline is the comparison method. Some podcast success-rate interpretations require checking against the original evaluation; they are not repeated here as established results.
vocab: Model-free learning
Learning behavior without an explicit learned dynamics model used for planning or imagined training.
Generalization
Performance beyond the examples or conditions used for learning.
Evaluation protocol
The exact rules used to obtain and compare results.
pages.cue: When you hear the Dreamer example, separate learning in a model, acting in an environment, and measuring success. Those are three different stages.

pages.title: Embodied intelligence: bodies, users, and transfer
pages.subtitle: PART 1 / Why acting changes the problem
sections: A body makes assumptions consequential

Embodied AI perceives and acts through a virtual or physical form. A robot, wearable assistant, and virtual avatar can have different senses, action possibilities, and failure consequences. A sensor measures something; an actuator produces an action. In the cup example, seeing a successful movement on screen and safely executing it with a real gripper are different achievements. [06.2, 06.4]
Physical and mental models

A physical world model represents objects, dynamics, and the consequences of actions. A mental world model, as discussed in the existing notes, represents aspects of a user's goals, beliefs, or intentions. Theory of mind is reasoning about another agent's mental state. A model's prediction about what someone wants remains an inference; it is not permission to act. Mixed initiative describes interaction where either the person or system may initiate a step.
Planning across levels

“Put the cup away” is a high-level goal. Reaching the shelf, positioning a gripper, and applying motor control operate at different levels. Hierarchical control connects those levels. A vision-language-action model (VLA) links visual and language inputs to actions. Such a policy may be combined with a world model and an outcome-scoring model. That is a design proposal to assess, not evidence that every combined system is dependable. [06.2]
The transfer problem

Simulation-to-real transfer, often called sim2real, concerns moving behavior learned in simulation to physical hardware. Real surfaces, friction, lighting, and sensor errors can differ from a simulator. This is one form of distribution shift: the conditions of use differ from those represented in training or evaluation. Imitation learning learns from demonstrations, including teleoperation, where a human remotely controls a robot. Demonstrations also have a limited coverage of situations.
A useful reading distinction

The embodied-agent material proposes several routes to better perception, planning, memory, and interaction. Keep the architecture diagram separate from the evidence for each component and from end-to-end deployment results. When you dip into a paper, look first for the actual task and environment, then ask which part of the proposed system was evaluated.
vocab: Zero-shot
Attempting a task without task-specific training examples in the claimed evaluation setting.
Partial observability
The system cannot directly observe every relevant aspect of the situation.
Working memory
Temporary state used during ongoing processing; different from lasting knowledge learned in weights.
pages.cue: For a wearable or robot example, ask what the system sensed, what it was allowed to do, and whether it was tested on real hardware or only in simulation.

pages.title: The alternative bet: smaller, structured intelligence
pages.subtitle: PART 2 / Combining learned patterns with explicit knowledge
sections: What “neurosymbolic” adds

Neurosymbolic AI combines neural learning with explicit structures such as rules, relations, or mathematical constraints. A neural network learns numerical parameters from data. A symbolic representation makes selected entities and relationships explicit. The existing notes present these approaches as potentially complementary to scaling, rather than proving that all large models should be replaced. [06.7]
A rule can reduce what must be learned

In the cup example, a rule that a blocked shelf cannot be used is explicit knowledge. A learned perception model could estimate whether the shelf is blocked; a separate constraint could govern the action. A knowledge graph represents entities and relationships as nodes and edges. A logical constraint states a relationship that an acceptable solution should satisfy. These structures can make particular requirements explicit, but incorrect rules or missing facts can still produce bad decisions.
Structure is an inductive bias

An inductive bias favors some solutions over others. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), for example, incorporate mathematical statements about physical behavior into learning. Compositionality is building more complex structures from reusable parts. Few-shot learning concerns learning from a small number of examples. The research question is whether the chosen structure reduces data or computation while preserving the capabilities the task needs. [06.7]
Distilling and checking

Distillation transfers aspects of a model's behavior or knowledge into another representation or model. Symbolic distillation seeks an explicit structure rather than only another network. Formal verification checks stated properties against a formal specification under defined assumptions. Passing such a check does not establish every real-world safety property, especially if the specification or connection to the physical world is incomplete.
Judge a bounded claim

Scaling laws describe empirical relationships between resources and measured performance. They are not guarantees about every useful capability. Equally, “smaller” is not a synonym for safer, more accurate, or cheaper in every setting. Ask: smaller by which measure, better on which task, compared with which baseline, and at what total system cost? Keep specific numerical comparisons tied to their original evaluation conditions.
vocab: Parameters versus rules
Learned numerical values and explicitly stated relationships play different roles.
Specification
A precise statement of the properties a system is intended to satisfy.
Interpretability
How a person can understand selected aspects of a system; it is not itself proof of correctness.
pages.cue: When the podcast presents an alternative to scaling, identify what structure is added and what evidence would show it helps beyond one selected demonstration.

pages.title: Reading independent safety evidence
pages.subtitle: PART 3 / From performance claims to warranted confidence
sections: What an assessment can tell you

An evaluation tests a capability or behavior under specified conditions. An independent assessment is conducted with some separation from the developer, but its value still depends on access, methods, incentives, and scope. A research synthesis brings together findings from multiple sources; it is not one new experiment. The research compendium uses the International AI Safety Report 2026 as a synthesis of capability developments and emerging risks. [06.11]
Capability does not come only from model size

Pre-training learns broad patterns from a large training dataset and produces a base model. Post-training further adapts it, for example through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or distillation. Inference is running a trained model. Inference-time compute is processing used while producing an answer or taking action. The compiled safety summary highlights post-training as an increasingly important source of capability gains. [06.11]
The benchmark-to-deployment gap

A benchmark score answers the question set by a particular test. A real deployment may involve different tools, longer tasks, unreliable inputs, and consequences not represented by that test. Data contamination occurs when evaluation material or related answers enter training data. Evaluation awareness concerns a system recognizing test conditions; gaming exploits features of an evaluation without achieving its intended purpose. These are reasons to examine how a score was obtained, not reasons to dismiss all benchmarks.
Break the conclusion into parts

Separate capability (what can be done), reliability (how consistently it is done), and safety (whether relevant harms are acceptably controlled in context). A system might be capable but unreliable, or reliably pursue an inappropriate objective. A threat model states the actors, assets, and failure scenarios being considered. A test result without that context is easy to overgeneralize.
Questions worth taking into the paper

Look for the task, model version, access and tools, comparison baseline, success definition, and conditions excluded from the claim. Identify the gap between the reported result and the use you are considering. This guide is teaching how to read existing conclusions; it has not rerun experiments or independently checked the original report.
vocab: Failure mode
A particular way a system can fail.
External validity
How far a result applies beyond the setting in which it was obtained.
Uncertainty
A limit on what the available evidence allows you to conclude.
pages.cue: When a striking percentage appears, pause and identify its denominator and test conditions. Do not carry it directly into a founder presentation without checking its source.

pages.title: Agents, control, and deployment boundaries
pages.subtitle: PART 3 / A fluent answer and a trustworthy action are different questions
sections: An agent adds an operating loop

An AI agent combines a model with a loop that can plan steps, use tools, observe results, and continue toward a goal. Autonomy concerns which decisions and actions it can take without human intervention. More tool access can expand both capability and the consequences of errors. A text-only answer, a code-executing assistant, and a robot moving an object present different problems. [06.11]
Useful categories of risk

The existing safety notes distinguish malicious use, where someone deliberately uses a system to cause harm; malfunctions, where the system fails or behaves unexpectedly; and systemic risks, which arise through widespread interaction with society and the economy. The categories can overlap. A strong capability can assist a defender or an attacker; the surrounding access and incentives matter.
Boundaries need implementation

Access control determines which resources a system may use. Least privilege gives it only the access needed for the task. A sandbox limits where code can run and what it can affect. A human approval gate reserves a specified action for a person. These are standard explanatory concepts, not claims that the R06 systems implement them successfully. A model saying it will obey a limit is different from an external mechanism enforcing that limit.
Memory is not automatic learning or accountability

A context window holds material available for the current model computation. A key-value cache (KV-cache) reuses internal computations over context; it is not a lasting record of verified knowledge. Retrieval brings stored material into a model's input. Persistent memory stores information across interactions. Any such memory can contain stale, incorrect, or untrusted material. Provenance records where information came from and how it was transformed.
Keep proposals labelled

The existing notes contain vendor and podcast ideas about composite architectures, agent identity, and hard constraints. They can prompt useful questions, but they should remain labelled as proposals. The compendium explicitly excludes the vendor memorandum from its core summary. Do not treat an appealing design story as an independently demonstrated safety guarantee. [06.1, 06.3]
vocab: Alignment
The problem of making a system's behavior fit intended goals and constraints.
Incident reporting
Recording observed failures so they can be investigated and learned from.
Monitoring
Observing behavior during operation; its usefulness depends on what it can detect and what follows.
pages.cue: When an agent is described as safe, ask what is enforced outside the model, what is merely requested in a prompt, and what evidence covers the whole operating loop.

pages.title: A reading route and one paper to start with
pages.subtitle: SYNTHESIS / Read, listen, inspect, and explain
sections: Bring the three questions back together

World models ask how a system can represent and anticipate its environment. Structured approaches ask what explicit knowledge can contribute alongside learning. Safety assessment asks what observations justify confidence in a particular use. None of these questions is settled by a polished demonstration alone. For a founder, the skill is moving between the mechanism, the evidence, and the decision without turning an attractive hypothesis into a promise.
One recommended first paper: DreamerV3

Start with Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models by Danijar Hafner and colleagues. It provides a concrete example of learning a world model and using imagined experience to improve behavior. Read the abstract and introduction, then inspect the method overview and results. Ask: what comes from real experience, what happens inside the model, and how is improvement measured? It is an anchor for the technical strand, not a substitute for the safety assessment or the neurosymbolic work. [06.5]
Use one stopping question at a time

After reading a topic, listen for its corresponding idea in the podcast. Pause when a claim becomes important or confusing, follow the relevant source bookmark, and look for the passage, figure, or evaluation that addresses it. You do not need to read every paper cover to cover before resuming. Explain the idea in your own words, then note what you still cannot establish. These are suggested reading actions; this guide has not performed them for you.
Keep the existing cautions visible

Podcast narratives can simplify mechanisms, omit evaluation conditions, or repeat a disputed numerical interpretation. Check important percentages, study attributions, and deployment claims against the cited source before relying on them. This guide draws on an existing compendium and vocabulary collection; it does not independently verify every underlying result. The expanded reference entries retain their inherited wording and qualifications.
vocab: Ask about mechanism
What would make the claimed effect happen?
Ask about evidence
Which result supports this exact claim, under which conditions?
Ask about application
What changes when the setting, user, tools, or consequences change?
pages.cue: Before moving on from R06, explain the robot example using a world model, a policy, a critic, a constraint, and an evaluation. Then identify one thing you would still want to check.

Proposes sequences of actions to the world model, optimizes them against the cost, and outputs the first action to the effectors

Trainable part of the cost module that predicts future intrinsic cost, learning from past states and costs retrieved from memory
In 06.3, a scalar measure of the agent's discomfort (low is good); the agent acts to minimize its average over time
Stores past, current and predicted world states with their intrinsic costs; the world model reads and updates it; compared to the vertebrate hippocampus
