The outputs that act on the world (motors, actuators) that receive the actor's chosen action
A module that can pass back gradient estimates of the cost, so the whole system can be trained and can plan by gradient methods
Classical control method (since the 1950s): predict the future with a forward model, pick the action sequence with lowest cost, execute the first action, repeat
A model that predicts the next state of the world from the current state and a considered action
A perception-action episode where a policy maps the state straight to an action with no world-model prediction; likened to Kahneman's System 1
A perception-action episode that plans through the world model and cost, like MPC; likened to System 2; reasoning here means energy minimization
The part of the actor that directly produces an action from the estimated world state without deliberate planning
The part of the actor that finds the action sequence minimizing estimated cost, using gradient methods or dynamic programming for discrete actions
A method to find an optimal action sequence by solving smaller sub-problems; 06.3 uses it when the action space is discrete
A hidden variable that stands for what is unknown or uncertain, letting a world model output several plausible futures instead of one
Representing the world coarsely or finely; higher levels ignore hard-to-predict detail and allow longer-term prediction
The world is not fully predictable, so a world model must represent many possible outcomes, not one
Basic expectations (gravity, inertia, object permanence) infants learn mostly by observation, with higher concepts built on lower ones
LeCun's broad sense of reasoning: constraint satisfaction, finding states or actions that minimize energy
The hypothesis that people and animals have one dynamically configurable world model, so knowledge is shared across tasks and enables reasoning by analogy
A design for how perception, memory, prediction, cost and action modules fit together; 06.3 proposes one in which all modules are differentiable

The real world cannot be back-propagated through, so cost gradients cannot flow from outcomes back to actions; they must be estimated by trying perturbed actions, which is slow and potentially dangerous
Classical reinforcement-learning approach: estimate how the cost changes by trying slightly perturbed actions in the world; the slow, risky route a world model is meant to avoid

terms.term: Mode-2 loop (perceive, propose, simulate, evaluate, plan, act, store)
terms.definition: Perceive the state; the actor proposes an action sequence; the world model simulates the resulting states; the cost scores them; gradients refine the actions; the first action is executed; states and costs are stored
Plan a sequence of T steps ahead, execute only the first action, then replan from the new state; 06.3's loop is classical MPC except the world model and cost are learned

Alternatives to gradient-based optimization of actions, needed when the action-cost mapping has discontinuities or actions are discrete: dynamic programming, combinatorial optimization, simulated annealing, tree search with pruning
Uncertainty because the world is itself random, so one state and action can lead to several outcomes
Uncertainty because the agent's state representation or training data is incomplete, so predictions are imperfect
Train a fast policy network to approximate the result of slow Mode-2 planning, so good actions come from one pass; the agent "compiles" planned skills into reactive behavior

Using slow deliberate planning to discover an action, then training the reactive policy on it by minimizing a divergence from the planned action; the agent can focus on only one complex task at a time
A probabilistic graphical model; 06.3 says the proposed architecture is one, with the cost modules acting as log factors
LeCun's claim that planning by simulating with a world model and optimizing the energy goes beyond classical logical or probabilistic reasoning
Design safeguard: the intrinsic cost is hard-wired and cannot be trained or externally modified, to prevent behavioral collapse or uncontrolled drift toward bad behaviors
Submodules of the cost (pain, hunger, curiosity, social drives, standing up to walk) whose weights the configurator adjusts so the agent focuses on different subgoals at different times
Infer the objective an expert appears to be optimizing from watching its behavior, producing a critic for Mode-2 behavior
Learning behavior from an expert; 06.3 lists it as one of four ways to specify an agent's behavior (program it, define an objective, supervise a policy, or imitate)
Specifying an objective rather than a behavior; 06.3 says this is simpler to engineer and more robust, since the agent can adapt to unexpected conditions
An actor-critic reinforcement-learning method; 06.3 says its critic training resembles how the critic here is trained
A memory retrieved by content, not address; here the intrinsic cost stores (time, state, energy) triplets and the critic reads them back
Learning from a single example; 06.3 says a key-value memory with good slot allocation can do this and still interpolate between keys
Humans plan at an abstract level and decompose high-level goals into subgoals, down to muscle control; a world model needs to represent plans at several time scales and abstraction levels
(1) diverse training data, since what is seen depends on actions taken; (2) representing multiple plausible outcomes; (3) predicting at several time scales and abstraction levels
A scalar function F(x,y) that is low when x and y are compatible and high when not; it can represent cases where many y fit one x, without having to generate y
A situation where several different outputs are all compatible with one input, such as many plausible continuations of a video clip
The surface of an EBM's energy values: low near data points, high away from them; contour lines mark level sets
Given part of an input plus a proposed rest, judge whether the completion is plausible; the basic idea of self-supervised learning in 06.3
Learn representations sx and sy of two inputs so both are maximally informative about their inputs and sy is easy to predict from sx, trading predictability against information
LeCun's hypothesis: predicting video in representation space would make edges, depth maps, occlusion and object permanence emerge, building a hierarchy of concepts
An energy model E(x,y,z) with a hidden variable z that parameterizes the possible relationships between x and the y that fit it; inference picks the z that minimizes energy
Finding the hidden z that best explains a pair (x,y) by minimizing energy (e.g. the camera motion between two views, or whether a car turned left or right); eliminating z leaves F(x,y)
Training failure where the energy surface goes flat and every y gets the same low energy, so the model says nothing; the core failure that non-contrastive methods must prevent

Per 06.3: plain predictors cannot collapse; generative latent-variable models collapse if z has too much capacity; auto-encoders collapse if the code is large enough to learn the identity; joint embeddings collapse if encoders output constants
A network that compresses an input to a code and reconstructs it; it can collapse by learning the identity function when the code has too much capacity
Two encoders map x and y to representations that are pushed to agree; can collapse if the encoders ignore inputs and emit identical constants
Train by pushing energy down on real pairs and up on made-up "contrastive" pairs; 06.3 argues the number of contrastive samples can grow exponentially with dimension, so it scales badly
The way requirements blow up as data dimension grows; LeCun's main reason to argue against contrastive methods

Push energy down on real data while a regularizer shrinks the volume of low-energy space, "shrink-wrapping" the data; LeCun says these are more promising long-term and can be combined with contrastive ones
Examples of contrastive loss functions: hinge loss with a distance-dependent margin; InfoNCE compares one true pair against K contrastive samples
06.3 lists Siamese nets, DrLIM, PIRL, MoCo, SimCLR, GANs, denoising and masked auto-encoders, and contrastive divergence as contrastive or near-contrastive approaches
Twin networks with shared weights trained on pairs (a distorted version versus another sample); the architecture behind many contrastive methods

Two encoders turn x and y into sx and sy; a predictor (optionally using a latent z) predicts sy from sx; energy is the prediction error in representation space; non-generative, so it need not predict every detail of y
JEPAs stacked so higher levels take lower-level representations and make longer-term, more abstract predictions; the basis for hierarchical planning under uncertainty
An encoder that maps many different inputs to the same representation, so they all get the same energy; one way a JEPA handles many compatible outcomes and drops irrelevant detail
Predicting an abstract encoding of the future instead of its raw pixels; ignores irrelevant detail like trees by the road or sidewalk texture
Non-contrastive criteria for training JEPAs that keep representations informative and prevent collapse without contrastive samples
Maximize information in sx about x; maximize information in sy about y; make sy predictable from sx; minimize information in the latent z; the first, second and fourth prevent collapse

Collapse where representations carry little information (constant codes) or where the latent can simply copy the answer; prevented by maximizing representation information and limiting latent capacity
Ways to stop z from doing all the work: make it discrete (VQ-VAE), low-dimensional, sparse (L1 norm) or noisy (VAE-style entropy)
Penalize the absolute size of a vector's entries so most are zero; restricts the low-energy region to low-dimensional manifolds
A generative auto-encoder with a noisy latent whose distribution is regularized; an example of limiting latent information
An EBM is defined without probabilities; the energy is the fundamental object, though it can be turned into a probability via a Gibbs distribution

A non-contrastive JEPA training method: an invariance term (prediction error) plus a variance term (keep each embedding component's spread above a threshold) and a covariance term (push correlations between components to zero), computed over a batch
A small trainable network that maps representations to higher-dimensional embeddings before VICReg's variance and covariance losses are applied
LeCun's contrast: VICReg makes the components of representations differ over a batch, while classic contrastive methods make different input samples differ and need many negative samples
The built-in preference set by encoder and predictor architecture about what information counts as predictable; extra prediction heads for task-relevant variables can steer it
Extra output layers trained to predict task-relevant, easily derived variables, used to bias a JEPA toward useful representations

LeCun argues generative latent-variable models cannot drop irrelevant detail except by pushing it into a latent, because they do not form abstract invariant representations of y; predicting every pixel (leaves, ripples, carpet texture) is impractical
Low-level representations carry detail for short-term prediction; high-level ones are coarser and enable long-term prediction; temporal pooling between levels coarse-grains the representation

A high-level cost sets abstract actions that act as conditions or subgoals for the lower level, which then finds low-level actions to satisfy them; optimizing all levels jointly is better than the greedy top-down pass
In hierarchical planning, a target or condition for the level below to satisfy, not a real motor command; old idea in control theory
A classical controller given a target state whose control is proportional to the negative gradient of the squared distance to that target

06.3 lists: intrinsic randomness; deterministic but chaotic; deterministic but partly observable; sensors give partial information; representation lacks needed information; model limited by representational power (bounded rationality); model trained on limited data
An agent's model being inaccurate because of limits on its representational power or computation
Moving a prediction's randomness into a latent variable so it can be optimized or sampled; 06.3 does not need it because latent parameterization is fundamental to its design

A penalty on the latent variable that limits its information; at planning time latents are sampled from the distribution it defines (via a Gibbs distribution), and the regularizer can be predicted from past states
With k possible discrete latent values and t time steps the number of predicted trajectories grows as k^t; directed search and pruning such as Monte-Carlo tree search are needed
Search strategies that explore only promising branches; 06.3 suggests them for discrete actions or latents; beam search and MCTS count as approximate dynamic programming
Choosing actions that minimize the average predicted cost, or the average plus its variance so as to minimize risk or uncertainty about the cost
Mechanisms where latent variables modulate which connections are used between frames or modules; suggested for the world model's low-level video prediction
A memory where a query is matched to keys, normalized, and used to read or update stored values; each entry can be the state of one entity (a bottle, the kitchen); all steps are differentiable

Passive observation; active foveation (steering attention); passive agency (watching others act); active egomotion (moving sensors); active agency (acting, which raises the exploration-exploitation dilemma)
The trade-off between trying new things to learn and using what already works; sharpest when the agent's own actions change what it observes
Intrinsic motivation modules that drive attention and exploration toward parts of the state space where the world model is inexact or uncertain

Infer optimal action sequences; produce configurations of latent variables for the unknown part of the world; train policy networks for Mode-1; in adversarial settings the latents are chosen to maximize cost
A network that learns distributions of latent variables so good, plausible latents can be sampled quickly instead of searched

Main controller that modulates other modules' parameters and connection graphs (routing signals, activating sub-networks, focusing attention); with transformers, its outputs can act as extra input tokens; needed for hardware reuse and knowledge sharing
Transformer blocks give the same result however objects are assigned to input tokens, which suits reasoning about interacting objects; extra input tokens can reconfigure the connection graph
Constraining attention to the past so a transformer predicts the next state, action and cost without seeing the future

06.3 warns that allowing complex modulation of the intrinsic cost could make the agent's basic drives hard to control, including cost terms that implement safety guardrails; hence the intrinsic cost stays immutable
A related hierarchical world-model and planning system trained end-to-end through reinforcement learning, cited as prior work on hierarchical planning
LeCun calls it a largely unsolved problem; most solutions need a predefined action vocabulary, whereas he wants intermediate action representations to be learned

Unproven: whether H-JEPA can be built and trained from video; how best to regularize the latent; how the actor infers actions and latents; how short-term memory represents beliefs; and the configurator, which he calls the most mysterious module; he expects many years of work
06.3 maps modules to brain areas: perception to sensory cortex, world model and critic to prefrontal cortex, intrinsic cost to amygdala, short-term memory to hippocampus; explicitly speculative

In 06.3 EBM means any model treating the energy function as fundamental and shaping its landscape by learning, broader than the probabilistic definition; the Boltzmann machine is an early contrastively trained example
Options if gradient-based planning fails on discrete or non-smooth problems

A reinforcement-learning algorithm of three networks trained together from replayed experience: a world model that predicts outcomes, a critic that judges their value, and an actor that picks actions; one fixed configuration reportedly beats specialized methods on 150+ tasks
Learning to act by interaction and reward; 06.5 notes it is also used to improve language models beyond their pretraining data
A standard, widely applicable RL algorithm used as the general-purpose baseline Dreamer is compared against
Settings of a learning algorithm tuned by hand per task; needing to retune them is the brittleness 06.5 says holds RL back; Dreamer uses fixed ones
Reward signals that arrive rarely (like collecting a diamond in Minecraft), making exploration and long-horizon credit hard
Benchmark task of collecting diamonds from scratch, hard due to sparse rewards, exploration difficulty, long horizons and procedural worlds; earlier methods used human data or curricula

Dreamer's actor and critic learn behavior purely from abstract trajectories of representations predicted by the world model; while acting in the environment, actions are sampled from the actor with no lookahead planning

Dreamer's world model: an encoder maps inputs to stochastic representations z; a sequence model with a recurrent state h predicts them from past actions; separate heads predict reward and episode continuation and reconstruct inputs
The combination of recurrent state h and representation z; the actor and critic operate on it, benefiting from the Markovian representations the world model learns
Compressing inputs into a compact code and reconstructing them; used so the world model's representations stay informative
A trick that lets gradients pass through a sampling step of discrete representations so the encoder can be trained end to end

Three terms minimized end to end: prediction loss (reconstruct inputs, predict reward and continuation), dynamics loss (sequence model predicts the next representation) and representation loss (make representations predictable), weighted 1, 1 and 0.1
A measure of how different two probability distributions are; used here to align predicted and actual representations
An operator that blocks gradient flow through one side of a loss; the dynamics and representation losses differ only in where it sits and their scale
Clip the KL losses below 1 nat (about 1.44 bits) so they switch off once well minimized, avoiding a degenerate solution where dynamics are trivial to predict but carry little information
Make categorical outputs a mix of 1% uniform and 99% network output so they can never become deterministic, preventing spikes in the KL losses

symlog(x)=sign(x)ln(|x|+1) squashes large positive and negative values while staying near the identity around zero; symexp is its inverse; used for observations and prediction targets so scale does not wreck learning
For rewards and returns the network outputs a softmax over exponentially spaced bins and is trained with cross entropy on a twohot target, so gradient size no longer depends on target size
Encode a number as weights on the two nearest bins (summing to 1), a generalization of one-hot to continuous values
The critic predicts a categorical distribution of returns, not one number, because returns can be multi-modal and vary by orders of magnitude across environments
A bootstrapped estimate of future return that blends predicted rewards with the critic's value estimates, so rewards beyond the prediction horizon (T=16) count; discount 0.997
Regularize the critic toward an exponentially moving average of its own parameters to stabilize learning, similar to target networks
Start the reward predictor and critic outputs at zero so large random early predictions do not delay learning
A bonus for keeping the actor's action choices varied so it keeps exploring; Dreamer uses a fixed scale of 3x10^-4 across domains

Divide returns by their 5th-to-95th percentile range (smoothed by moving average), scaling down only large returns; keeps exploration right whether rewards are sparse or dense, outlier-robust, with fixed hyperparameters
A policy-gradient estimator used for discrete and continuous actions in Dreamer's actor loss
The world model rolls forward from a few context frames and the action sequence without seeing intermediate images; Dreamer predicts 45 frames from 5 context images in DMLab and a quadruped robot
Atari, ProcGen, DMLab, robot locomotion and manipulation, plus non-visual domains and Minecraft, spanning 150+ tasks

An experiment that removes one component to see how much it mattered; Dreamer's ablations show the world model's KL objective matters most, then return normalization and symexp twohot, and that it rests mainly on the unsupervised reconstruction signal, not reward gradients

How little interaction an agent needs; on DMLab Dreamer at 100M frames beat IMPALA and R2D2+ at 1B steps, a data-efficiency gain of over 1000%, though those baselines were not designed for data efficiency

Six sizes from 12M to 400M parameters learned with fixed hyperparameters; bigger models scored higher and needed less interaction; a higher replay ratio (more gradient updates per environment step) also helps
Infinite random 3D worlds, up to 36,000 steps (30 minutes), 12 items to discover from sparse rewards; all Dreamer agents found diamonds within 100M steps while baselines stopped at the iron pickaxe
A Minecraft agent trained by behavioral cloning on contractors' keyboard and mouse data then fine-tuned with RL, using 720 GPUs for 9 days, versus Dreamer's 1 GPU for 9 days without human data
Training an agent to copy an expert's recorded actions; needs expert data, unlike Dreamer
A Minecraft agent that reaches similar depth in the tech tree by making API calls to a language model on top of a hand-engineered scripting layer exposing high-level actions
One large model fitted to expert demonstrations across many tasks; only applicable where expert data exists
A planning algorithm using a learned value-prediction model for board games and Atari; 06.5 says the implementation was not released and is complex to reproduce
Popular continuous-control algorithm that reuses experience for data efficiency but needs tuning, especially its entropy scale, and struggles with high-dimensional inputs
Working out which earlier actions caused a later reward; one of the capabilities tested by the BSuite benchmark

Atari (57 games), ProcGen (16 games with randomized levels), DMLab (30 3D tasks), Atari100k (26 games, 400K frames), Proprio Control (18 tasks), Visual Control (20), BSuite (23 environments, 468 configurations); Dreamer set new state of the art on several
An Atari simulator setting where actions sometimes repeat, to prevent agents exploiting determinism
Each Dreamer agent trained on a single Nvidia A100 GPU and an implementation is public, so many research labs can reproduce it
Clip each tensor's gradient when it exceeds 30% of the L2 norm of its weight matrix, so the clipping threshold no longer depends on the loss scale
Normalizes gradients by RMSProp first and then applies momentum (Adam computes both on raw gradients); allows a smaller epsilon and avoided occasional instabilities seen with Adam
Dreamer's sequence model: a GRU whose recurrent weights are block-diagonal (8 blocks), giving many memory units without a quadratic rise in parameters and compute
Stored past trajectories reused for training; Dreamer uses a uniform replay buffer with an online queue and stores latent states so the world model can be initialized on replayed data
The fraction of time steps trained on per step collected; e.g. 32 on Atari with action repeat 4 and batch 16x64 is one gradient step every 128 environment steps; trades compute for data efficiency
Sampling replayed experience by importance; it improved Dreamer too, but uniform replay was used for ease of implementation
Zero-initializing the output weights of twohot distributions so the untrained agent does not predict made-up rewards and values
Stride-2 convolutions compress images to a small grid and transposed convolutions reconstruct them; vector inputs use symlog and 3-layer MLPs
Normalization and activation function choices introduced in DreamerV3's network architecture
DreamerV1 handled continuous control, V2 surpassed human performance on Atari, V3 learns out of the box across diverse benchmarks with robustness techniques, a block GRU, AGC and LaProp
Same values everywhere (no annealing, prioritized replay, weight decay or dropout); results use 5-10 seeds with error bars; DMLab baselines were given a 10x data advantage at 1B steps
12M to 400M parameters derived from one model dimension; 200M default; on the control suites the 12M model matched performance, making it accessible to small labs

A sparse-reward environment rewarding 12 milestones (log, plank, stick, crafting table, wooden pickaxe, cobblestone, stone pickaxe, iron ore, furnace, iron ingot, iron pickaxe, diamond), each once per episode

06.5's supplementary figure says at the 100M-step budget Dreamer obtains diamonds in 0.4% of episodes, which the authors call a challenge for future research; every trained agent found a diamond eventually, but it is rare per episode (the audio's "mastered" framing overstates this)

A planner for learned world models: lifts the trajectory into virtual states so optimization runs in parallel across time, adds Gaussian noise to the state iterates for exploration, and reshapes gradients to avoid brittle state-input gradients; still optimizes states, not "abandoning" them (the audio overstates this)

A learned model that, given current state and a sequence of future actions, predicts what happens next, approximating the environment's true conditional distribution; the post notes the term is overloaded (explicit dynamics model versus implicit internal state in a generative model, e.g. an LLM's board representation when playing chess)
Because a world model is differentiable you can roll it forward under hypothetical action sequences and backpropagate through the predictions
The simplest planner: roll the model forward from the start state under an action sequence and minimize the error between the final state and the goal
Differentiating through a model applied to itself repeatedly; over long horizons it leads to exploding or vanishing gradients
The Jacobian's conditioning grows exponentially with horizon T, so gradients to early actions explode or vanish; the first of three long-horizon pain points
Long tasks need non-greedy moves (going around a wall, backing up) and the search space grows with horizon, so the loss surface is rough with many traps; the second pain point

Treat the dynamics as a soft penalty and optimize actions and states together; shares the same global minimizers as rollout planning, evaluates all T steps in parallel, and replaces a deep product of Jacobians with a sum
The gradient of a world model's output with respect to its state input; 06.9 calls it untrustworthy, adversarial and brittle for deep-learning models
The gradient with respect to action input; reasonable to optimize because the action space is low-dimensional and densely trained
Tiny input changes along a model's gradient can flip its output (adversarial examples); appears in vision, LLMs and RL; there is a known trade-off between robustness and performance

Training data lies near a low-dimensional manifold; training controls behavior along it but not in orthogonal (normal) directions, where the model can be very sharp, so states can be nudged to fool it
A bound on how fast a function's output can change with its input; reasonable along the data manifold, very high in normal directions
GRASP's loss that blocks gradients into the world model's state input; alone it fails (trivial minima), so a dense goal term is added
A goal-distance penalty applied across the trajectory to restore the goal signal to earlier states; balanced against the dynamics loss so it does not become purely greedy
Gaussian noise added to virtual state updates so the planner can hop between basins; actions stay gradient-guided; not truly Langevin dynamics because actions are not noised
Every K_sync iterations GRASP rolls out from the real start state and takes a few gradient steps on the serial loss to keep states grounded; a serial planner such as CEM could replace it
A robot pushing-task benchmark where GRASP reports higher success and faster median time at longer horizons; the post gives no numbers in the readable text
A model whose next-state prediction depends only on a recent window of states and the current action; assumed for simplicity
Named as an extension: deeper diffusion timesteps can be viewed as smoothed versions of the world model
First-person video from the agent's own viewpoint; reveals intention (where you look) but hides the body's own motion, so models must infer consequences of invisible physical actions

terms.term: PEVA (Predicting Egocentric Video from human Actions)
terms.definition: A model that, given past frames and a desired change in 3D body pose, predicts the next first-person video frame; can generate atomic actions, counterfactuals and long videos
Conditioning on both locomotion (feet) and manipulation (hands); 06.10 uses a 48-dimensional action vector (3 root translation plus 15 upper-body joints x 3 rotations)
The hierarchy of body joints used to encode actions as relative joint rotations; positions are converted to a pelvis-centered local frame for invariance
Independent ways a body can move; full-body human motion spans 48+, making human control high-dimensional and structured
PEVA's backbone: a diffusion transformer that denoises a target frame from noise, conditioned on past context frames and actions, rolled forward frame by frame
A generative model that starts from noise and progressively denoises it into the target; here applied to video frames in latent space
The base design from Navigation World Models that PEVA extends with random timeskips, sequence-level training and whole-body action embeddings
Training trick that lets the model learn both short-term motion dynamics and longer-term activity patterns
Applying the loss over every frame prefix so the model learns whole motion sequences
All actions at a time step are concatenated into one vector that conditions each adaptive layer-norm layer, handling high-dimensional whole-body motion
Variational autoencoder components that compress frames into latent states and decode predicted latents back into pixels
Predict the next frame from context plus current action, append it, drop the oldest frame, repeat for each action; PEVA shows coherent 16-second rollouts
Decomposed movements (hand up/down/left/right, body forward/rotation) used to test whether the model understands how joint-level movement changes the egocentric view
Imagining what the view would look like had a different action been taken; one of PEVA's demonstrated abilities
Plan by simulating candidate action sequences and scoring them by perceptual similarity (LPIPS) to a goal image; the cross-entropy method (CEM) optimizes arm actions; framed as energy minimization
A learned perceptual image-similarity metric, used to score how close a simulated outcome is to the goal image
Fréchet Inception Distance, a measure of how realistic generated images are compared with real ones; compared across models and horizons
A large dataset pairing real-world egocentric video with body motion capture, used to train PEVA

Planning covers only simulated arm actions, no long-horizon or full-trajectory optimization, no closed-loop control, no explicit semantic goals, and image similarity is only a proxy objective; the authors call it an initial step

Empirical regularities that capability rises with more data, compute and parameters; 06.7 says the resulting race is unsustainable and gatekeeps AI to firms that can afford it; Gemini Ultra's training is estimated at $191 million and data centers at up to 3.7% of global greenhouse emissions

Richard Sutton's argument that general methods that scale with computation have beaten approaches built on human domain knowledge, so leveraging computation is what matters in the long run; 06.7 argues for a more nuanced view
When the cost of training and using state-of-the-art models exceeds what researchers outside large tech companies can afford, and models are released closed-source, raising trustworthiness concerns
06.7's contrast: the human brain runs on about 20 W (about 3.15 MWh over 18 years) while GPT-3 needed 1.287 GWh to train, yet the brain generalizes from far fewer data points
Transistor counts doubled roughly every 2 years while Dennard scaling kept power density roughly constant; AI parameters double about every 6 months with no such energy counterweight

Integrating data-driven neural networks with symbolic reasoning (logic, knowledge graphs, differential equations) to cut the data, parameters and compute needed while keeping generalization; 06.7 presents it as complementary to scaling, not a replacement

If high-dimensional training data shares simple features, learned representations lie on smooth lower-dimensional surfaces (manifolds); networks do well on smooth manifolds and need lots of data and parameters to smooth out sharp regions
A network with enough parameters can be trained to find a suitable manifold representation; together with the manifold hypothesis it underlies why scaling works
Sharp regions in the loss landscape or data manifold; unavoidable in practice (hence sharpness-aware training) and the reason purely data-driven models need so much scale

06.7's proposed training loop: after gradient updates lift the neural representation to a symbolic one, reason symbolically across sharp regions, then project back onto a smooth submanifold where small networks suffice
Networks whose loss includes known physics written as partial differential equations (PDEs); related: physics-informed neural operators and differentiable simulation
A differentiable-simulation approach that parameterizes PDE terms with small neural networks and fits them to video, generalizing to new geometries and conditions from a single video
Neural radiance fields augmented with physics-based material point methods follow conservation laws and render about 2 orders of magnitude faster than baselines
A graph of semantic relations among objects used to improve accuracy and cut training data; Amazon's COSMO uses LLMs to build common-sense knowledge graphs for recommendations
Extracting symbolic representations from a neural network's continuous space; an open research area
Weights or activations take discrete values (integers or binary); QLoRA quantizes to 4 bits; such discrete codes can be read as atomic propositions to extract symbolic structures
Classical technique to extract symbolic graphs (finite automata, knowledge graphs) from observations of discrete states; used to learn a small finite-state machine from a quantized recurrent network
Check a model's outputs against formal specifications by model checking, rank them by how many properties they satisfy, and use that ranking as a reward signal for fine-tuning
Distilling common-sense knowledge from GPT-3 into a knowledge graph and a neural model reported as 100 times smaller with better common-sense reasoning
Models such as OpenAI's o3 that scale training- and inference-time compute, with techniques like chain-of-thought; 06.7 notes its focus is training-phase scaling

A neurosymbolic framework that distills an LLM into a hidden Markov model that reasons about logical constraints (as deterministic finite automata); a 7B LLM plus 2B HMM beat GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 by over 30% in a human study of constraint adherence
A tractable probabilistic model of hidden states evolving over time; here used for efficient reasoning about logical constraints
A simple machine that accepts or rejects sequences by moving through a fixed set of states; used to encode logical constraints

A system co-designing networks and conservation-law equations for off-road driving that matched state of the art with 0.1% of the training time, 1% of the data and 96.9% fewer parameters, and with more training improved 46%
Learning novel objects from a handful of examples; using symbolic knowledge gave models about 95% smaller than the best neural-only baseline while beating it by 2%
Automatically extracts a knowledge graph from a text corpus and feeds it into retrieval-augmented generation to improve an LLM's output
Unlike one-block deep nets, a knowledge graph separates data, representation and tasks, so it is reusable, interpretable and expandable by users
Translate logical constraints into differentiable loss terms so symbolic knowledge is embedded during training while staying fully differentiable
Cited work argues large neural models lack true reasoning and lean on statistical patterns that do not generalize even within a family of reasoning tasks

Cognitive psychology idea of two modes: slow-learned, fast, automatic implicit processing (system 1) and quick-to-learn, slow-to-apply explicit symbolic reasoning (system 2); the two complement each other
Symbolic knowledge is compositional, so a few rules cover many situations, like grammar over sentences; it gets an agent near good solutions when outside familiar territory

The bitter lesson's classic case (AlphaGo Zero's move 37 found without human tactics) versus a counterexample: AlphaStar bootstrapped from 987,000 replays of the top 22% of players and its ablation without them did much worse
There may not be enough data in principle to sustain data-driven gains, and edge and low size, weight and power systems cannot scale data and compute, so strong inductive biases are needed
Small rules such as "carry the 1" that put a learner in a space where it can generalize; 06.7 says discovery and prior knowledge are not mutually exclusive

Second edition (2026) of a multi-country expert synthesis chaired by Yoshua Bengio, 100+ experts, advisers nominated by 30+ countries and bodies (OECD, EU, UN); it summarizes evidence and does not make policy recommendations
The report's scope: models and systems able to perform a wide variety of tasks across contexts (text, images, audio, other data) and often adapted to domain-specific uses

The 2026 report's narrowed focus: risks that arise at the frontier of AI capabilities, such as misuse, issues of control and cybersecurity; it leaves out bias, environmental impact, privacy and copyright covered in 2025
The leading edge of AI capability where, per the Bletchley Declaration, particular safety risks arise

terms.term: dangerous capability thresholds and if-then commitments
terms.definition: Risk-management practices the report highlights: set capability thresholds and commit to specific safety actions if a model crosses them; plus model evaluations
New in 2026: scenarios and forecasts (from the OECD and Forecasting Research Institute) to show policymakers the range of plausible outcomes under uncertainty

The report's central problem: AI capability moves fast but evidence on risks is slow and hard to assess, so acting too early can entrench ineffective rules and waiting for proof can leave society exposed

Leading systems excel at hard tasks (gold-level IMO math, expert science questions) yet fail simple ones (counting objects in an image, reasoning about physical space, recovering from basic errors in long workflows)

Further refining a base model for specific uses: supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, distillation; moderately compute-intensive and highly labour-intensive; now a main source of capability gains besides larger pre-training
Letting a model use more computing power while answering, generating intermediate steps before a final answer; produced big gains on mathematics, software engineering and science reasoning

A model trained to produce explicit intermediate reasoning steps (chains of thought) at inference, decomposing tasks; needs more compute at use and in training and can fail with irrelevant or repetitive chains
Reward outputs that match human preferences and penalise those that do not; one of two main subcategories of RL in post-training
RL for tasks with checkable answers such as maths or code, where correctness provides the reward

Train a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher's outputs; DeepSeek-V3 was reportedly fine-tuned from R1's reasoning outputs for roughly $10,000, and some work used as few as 1,000 teacher examples; it cannot advance the frontier but speeds proliferation
First, data- and compute-intensive stage (weeks or months on tens or hundreds of thousands of GPUs or TPUs) on billions or trillions of examples, producing a base model
Artificially generated data that mimics real data, increasingly used to make post-training less labour-intensive

A model (e.g. GPT-5) becomes a system (e.g. ChatGPT) when combined with other models, a chat interface, content filters, web access and integrations; deployment makes the system available while model release shares the base model as open-weight or closed-weight

Open-weight models have downloadable parameters; they bring research and commercial benefits but cannot be recalled, their safeguards are easier to remove and use outside monitored environments is hard to prevent or trace

Models learn from data by adjusting connection strengths (weights) between layered neurons; most leading models use the transformer, whose attention mechanism focuses on the most relevant parts of the input
Software built around a model (tools, memory, computer interface, web browser) that lets agents plan, pursue goals and act with less human oversight
A model configured to iteratively plan, reason and use tools to pursue goals specified in natural language; increasingly capable but prone to basic errors; examples include coding and research agents
Using many processors, servers or data centres together reduces dependence on large centralized compute, letting less well-resourced actors build and run powerful systems
Used two ways: the count of calculations a processor can do (FLOP/s) or the hardware (GPUs) that does them
Malicious use, malfunctions and systemic risks; "systemic" here means risks from widespread deployment across society and the economy, not the EU AI Act's narrower sense

AI can find software vulnerabilities and write malicious code; in one competition an agent identified 77% of the vulnerabilities in real software; the report says whether attackers or defenders gain more is uncertain

In 2025 multiple developers released new models with extra safeguards because pre-deployment testing could not rule out that they might meaningfully help novices develop weapons; the report says it released with safeguards, not that deployments were delayed
Scenarios where AI systems operate outside anyone's control with no clear path to regaining it; current systems lack the capabilities but are improving in autonomous operation
Models increasingly distinguish test settings from real deployment and exploit loopholes in evaluations, so dangerous capabilities could go undetected before deployment
The tendency to trust AI output without enough scrutiny; early evidence that reliance on AI tools can weaken critical thinking

Threat modelling to find vulnerabilities, capability evaluations to assess dangerous behaviors and incident reporting; 12 companies published or updated Frontier AI Safety Frameworks in 2025; mostly voluntary
Layering multiple safeguards so no single failure is decisive; harmful outputs still sometimes obtainable by rephrasing or splitting requests into smaller steps
Measures to absorb and recover from AI incidents that risk management will not prevent: stronger critical infrastructure, tools to detect AI-generated content, institutional capacity

At least 700 million weekly users of leading systems; over 50% of people in some countries but likely under 10% across much of Africa, Asia and Latin America; coding agents reliably complete tasks of about 30 minutes, up from under 10 minutes a year earlier

Four OECD scenarios from stagnation to acceleration; progress could plateau (data or energy bottlenecks), continue, or accelerate if AI speeds up AI research; developers announced hundreds of billions of dollars in data centre investment
Fluent, confident output that includes false statements, such as non-existent citations or facts; it makes safe adoption hard in high-stakes settings and invites over-reliance

Benchmarks often overstate real-world ability: tests are outdated, narrow, affected by data contamination, run in controlled labs, and one study found AI code still needed major human cleanup before use; an "evaluation science" is emerging to fix this
When a model was trained on the same questions used to test it, inflating scores by memorization; most developers do not track or disclose it

MMLU (undergraduate exams, leaders over 90%), GPQA and GPQA Diamond (graduate-level science, over 80%, exceeding PhD experts), International Mathematical Olympiad (gold-level, 5 of 6 problems), SWE-bench Verified, MATH, FrontierMath, AIME 24

The maximum length of software task (in human time) an AI agent finishes at 80% success; roughly 30 minutes now, doubling about every seven months; extrapolated to hours by 2027-2028 and days by 2030, though 80% is below professional standards and real work is messier
The best agents reach only 50% success on tasks of just over two hours; 80% needs tasks of roughly 25 minutes; agents lose track of progress and a website pop-up can derail a task

A foundation model that follows natural-language instructions, interprets multimodal sensor data and outputs motor commands (e.g. pi0.5, Gemini Robotics); still poor with unusual objects and unexpected events
Performance is highest in English; across 83 languages non-Latin-script and low-resource languages score lower; one study found 79% right on everyday US culture versus 12% on Ethiopian culture
Developers using AI assistants finished some tasks 20-30% faster on average, yet one study found experienced programmers were 19% slower on complex tasks while believing they were faster

Frontier training compute has grown about 5x per year (over 10^26 FLOP; about 125-fold more feasible by 2030); algorithmic efficiency improves 2-6x per year; datasets grow about 2.5x per year; frontier runs cost about $500 million, next generation $1-10 billion
Sudden jumps in a skill rather than gradual gains as models scale (e.g. adding large numbers once prompted to work step by step); researchers cannot yet say whether these become forecastable

Possible feedback loop where AI speeds up AI research; forecasters gave a median 20% (experts) or 8% (superforecasters) chance of compressing six years of progress into two; AI agents beat humans at two-hour research-engineering tasks but not eight-hour ones
If AI revenue fails to justify investments of hundreds of billions, scaling spending could be cut, putting a ceiling on progress and shifting gains to algorithms

Capability outruns adoption: healthcare AI may need 3-5 more years for approval and integration; autonomous vehicles will likely stay limited in 2030; small and medium enterprises (60% of workers) face expertise, infrastructure and cost barriers

Four plausible futures: progress stalls (analogue: aircraft speed plateau), slows (antibiotic discovery), continues (Moore's law) or accelerates (DNA sequencing), the last with AI comparable to human-level remote workers
Letting models form long-term memories and learn from user interaction during use; flagged as a key development area and a missing ability in the slower scenarios
Limited public knowledge of how advanced models are built, safeguarded, evaluated and deployed, especially internally deployed systems; low transparency hampers independent research and oversight

A study of 17 models: each 10x increase in training compute raised persuasiveness by about 1.8 percentage points; in experiments AI matched or beat non-expert humans at changing beliefs (e.g. trivia: +17 points after AI versus +9 after humans); real-world effects remain unproven. This is the "Hackenburg" study, separate from the 77% deepfake-text figure

Two different statistics: an AI agent identified 77% of the vulnerabilities in real software in one competition; and participants misidentified GPT-4o text as human-written 77% of the time after a five-minute conversation; the audio blends these with other claims
Manipulation influences someone without their full awareness; rational persuasion uses honest arguments they can endorse; the line is contested among researchers
A model telling users what they want to hear; rising evidence it has manipulative effects, alongside engagement-optimized AI companions that can foster dependence and reinforce harmful beliefs
Chat services with tens of millions of users, a small share of whom show increased loneliness, emotional dependence or delusions; investigations into severe incidents were ongoing
Documented but not widespread: only about 1% of flagged misleading social-media content is classed as AI-generated, and distribution costs and competing viewpoints weaken lab effects

Detection tools lag generation (benchmarks about 50% worse on real-world fakes); warning labels raised spotting accuracy only from 10.7% to 21.6%; watermarking and content logs help but can be removed or raise privacy concerns; signed metadata on authentic media is a complement
The OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor and AI Incident Database collect reported cases; the main evidence for harms from fake content, so prevalence is unreliable and underreported
Errors compounding across generations when models train on synthetic data in domains where answers are hard to verify; verifier models are an untested idea to extend synthetic data further
About 10^13 tokens of high-quality public text exist and models approach it; image, video and sensor data add far more raw tokens but carry less meaning per item, needing new techniques

Frontier training runs in 2030 may need 4-16 GW; Stargate is planned at 1.2 GW; experts' median is 7.4% of US electricity for AI by 2030; the report says energy is unlikely to block scaling before the decade ends
A fab takes 3-5 years to build; one company may hold 10-40% of AI data-centre chips; 100,000x GPT-4's compute is feasible by 2030 versus the 10,000x implied by current growth
Unpublished, mathematician-vetted problems in three tiers (about 25% olympiad-level, 50% graduate, 25% research-level); AI scored under 2% in 2024 and about 25% (GPT-5) later using inference-scaling

Predictable links between size, compute and performance across six orders of magnitude, but empirical not guaranteed, predicting technical metrics not value; OpenAI discontinued GPT-4.5 despite gains matching them
Compute needed for equal performance falls about 2-6x per year (estimates about 3x); at the top end equal capability could need 10-100x less compute by 2030

An AI instantiated in a visual, virtual or physical form (avatar, wearable, robot) that perceives and acts in its surroundings; web-only agents and tele-operated or pre-programmed robots do not count as embodied by 06.2's definition

Avatars or android faces that convey emotion for therapy, metaverse guides, studio characters, education and customer service; Meta's Motivo controls a physics-based humanoid avatar zero-shot from poses, motions or objectives

An AI on a worn device (e.g. smart glasses) whose cameras and microphones give an egocentric view; it is embodied from the user's perspective; roles are coaching (physical tasks) and tutoring (mental tasks)

A general-purpose agent controlling a robot body (humanoid or arm on wheels) through senses such as cameras, tactile, force and audio; aimed at labor shortages, disaster rescue, elderly care and hospitals
The idea that robots interacting with the real world may be the only route to a general agent that reasons about the real world; described as an active area of scientific investigation
A model of objects and their properties, spatial relationships, dynamics and causal relationships between actions and outcomes grounded in physics
A model of the user: goals, intentions, emotions, social dynamics, cultural norms and verbal and non-verbal communication, so agents can anticipate needs and infer belief discrepancies
06.2 says world models enable reasoning and planning, zero-shot task completion, human-in-the-loop active learning and efficient exploration

06.2's critique: models that predict the next token or pixel are inefficient in size and carry too many textual or visual details while missing what reasoning and planning need, motivating predictive world models

Prompting language or vision-language models to plan is limited by inaccuracy and hallucination; on Meta's WordPrediction benchmark LLMs and diffusion models did poorly, VLMs better but still hallucinated action plans
Meta's vision encoder trained with a contrastive vision-language objective, giving general visual embeddings across many tasks without task-specific pretraining
A large model that controls an agent's body to solve many tasks zero-shot; e.g. Meta Motivo for a simulated humanoid

Models of two-person interaction (active listening, visual synchrony, turn-taking) trained on the Seamless Interaction dataset of over 4,000 hours; generate face and body motion responding to audio-visual input
Using machine learning to detect and respond to human emotions; a base technology for virtual embodied agents
An agent acting proactively under changing intentions instead of only reacting to prompts; needed for coaching and tutoring
Training vision-language models to predict what a wearer wants to achieve from egocentric context

Meta's open vision-language model built on the perception encoder with an LLM; reports gains of +9.1 points on perception-focused image tasks, +39.8 CIDEr on video captioning and +3.8 on fine-grained video QA without distilling from proprietary models
A metric that scores generated captions against human reference captions; used for video captioning

Noise robustness, speech variability (accents, separating the wearer from bystanders), limited compute on wearables, tool use and factuality; edge AI (local processing) would cut latency and ease privacy worries
A general-purpose encoder for touch signals enabling force estimation, slip detection, texture recognition and grasp stability prediction; touch helps when vision is occluded

Imagine how the environment evolves under alternative actions, score the futures and pick the lowest-cost sequence; costlier than calling a policy (System 1) but more likely to generalize zero-shot outside the training distribution

Behavior cloning only imitates what it has seen; reinforcement learning needs trial and error in the real world and verifiable rewards that are hard to gather; a reusable world model enables zero-shot planning
A world model must handle low-level dynamics (joint torques every few milliseconds) and human-scale actions (insert the battery) lasting seconds or minutes

Pixel-generating models are expressive but expensive; LLM text plans hallucinate from spurious correlations; joint-embedding models forecast in abstract latent space and are efficient and stable, but only as good as their abstraction of the task's causal structure

An action-conditioned JEPA video world model for robot planning: encode context frames, roll out a predictor with actions, and optimize actions so the last imagined state embedding is close (L1 distance) to the goal image embedding; commands are end-effector position deltas
Learned world models send commands (end-effector or centroid targets) at under 20 Hz to higher-frequency controllers that compute joint torques, like muscle-level control
A non-gradient way to optimize action sequences by sampling and refining, used when the learned model is not differentiable

Planning over symbolic or linguistic abstractions ("the drawer is open") that shrinks the search space and improves generalization; hard because procedural tasks are too varied to simulate and there is no objective measure of plausibility

An agent's ability to represent others' mental states (beliefs, goals, intentions, emotions, attention, memory); 06.2 argues mental world models are essential for tutoring, assistance and multi-agent collaboration
ToMi and Hi-ToM track mental states with restricted actions; ExploreToM adversarially generates belief-reasoning tasks by programmatic scene construction
A JEPA-style vision-language world model that predicts abstract representations of future world states instead of noisy, high-volume raw observations
An agent that knows not just what to show or tell but when, proactively and also on request, rather than only user-initiated prompting

Fixed memory (the weights, slow to write, fixed capacity); working memory (activations such as RNN or state-space-model state and the transformer KV-cache, fast but growing linearly); external memory (retrieval-augmented generation; chain of thought as external working memory)
A transformer's cache of key-value activations that acts as working memory; immutable and fast to use but it grows linearly with interaction time
A new scalable memory that grows sublinearly while the agent interacts, enabling personalization and life-long learning; 06.2 cites it as a research objective, not a solved capability
Lightweight ways to personalize a model by adding small trainable modules; fine-tuning trades new knowledge against forgetting and does not add capacity

Letting a model keep learning after deployment, currently blocked because resources grow linearly with interaction time; test-time training and forward-read-write methods with local update rules are candidate routes
55,000 multiple-choice video questions with near-identical video pairs needing different answers to block shortcuts; top models score 40.2% versus humans 92.9% and a 25% random guess
A violation-of-expectation benchmark of intuitive physics (permanence, immutability, spatio-temporal continuity, solidity); models often score near chance while humans approach ceiling
Test paradigm from developmental psychology showing physically plausible versus impossible events to see if a model registers the impossible one
Video question answering about causality with counterfactual, hypothetical, anticipation, planning and descriptive questions; models lag humans most on anticipation and hypothetical reasoning

A benchmark of procedural planning: identify the action between initial and final states (WM) or pick the right action sequence among distractors (PP), using action equivalents to avoid perceptual shortcuts

A language model that generates spoken dialogue; its output can guide a motion model either cascaded (via the generated speech) or via a codebook (adapters on its hidden states predict emotion and gesture codes)

A diffusion transformer trained with a flow-matching objective, conditioned on tokens from both speakers' audio (optionally the user's visual features), outputting Imitator face features and SMPL-H body features usable in 2D or 3D

Subjective pairwise human studies on 10 dimensions (lifelikeness, clarity of intent, turn-taking, listening, speaking) plus automatic metrics: lip-sync scores (Sync-C, Sync-D), FID for faces, Fréchet Gesture Distance (FGD) for bodies, and diversity
The idea that a wearable agent sees and hears what the wearer does, enabling ambient intelligence that stays context-aware without constant prompting

A wearable agent models both the physical environment and the user's mental state, planning over extended periods and adapting to changing circumstances; backed by contextual goal prediction plus a planner

A predictive model trained on unlabelled video that outputs interleaved natural-language descriptions of actions and resulting world states; on Visual Planning for Assistance benchmarks it reports +20% success rate, +10% mean action accuracy and +4% mIoU versus prompting baselines, and its system-2 plans were preferred in PlannerArena

JEPA planners forecast in latent video space, giving gradient-based trajectory optimization and fast test-time MPC but less interpretability; VLWM is interpretable language; 06.2 proposes contrasting the two

348 participants, 3,477 recordings with ground-truth goals across visual, audio, digital and longitudinal context; humans scored 93% multiple choice versus 84% for the best VLM, and models produced relevant goals only 55% of the time in the generative setting
Built on a partially observable semi-MDP; humans near perfect while the best models reach 57% on the world-model task and 38% on procedural planning

Locomotion (legged movement), navigation (planning to a goal given as coordinates, images or text), and dexterous manipulation (fine multi-finger control, still open); "full body control" learns them jointly
Action generalization (new tasks and skills), embodiment generalization, and visual/semantic generalization (new environments and objects); plus efficient lifelong adaptation without forgetting

Moving a policy trained in simulation to real hardware; limited by low scene variability and imprecise simulator physics; with reward specification and multi-task scaling it is a main bottleneck of deep RL for robots
Human demonstrations recorded by remote-controlling a robot, used to train folding-laundry style skills; high-quality data is a bottleneck and skills stay near the training settings

terms.term: policies plus world models plus scoring models
terms.definition: 06.2's proposed combination: a VLA policy, a task-agnostic world model and a task-conditioned cost model, so the world model can detect when the policy would fail and re-plan
Classical robotics stacks analytical models at different frequencies (e.g. a humanoid backflip), the same MPC idea that learned world models would plug into

Offline benchmarks (reproducible, not end to end), simulation benchmarks (MuJoCo, pyBullet; reproducible but not photoreal) and real-world hardware tests (the gold standard but costly and hard to reproduce); evaluation-on-hardware services use learned success classifiers or human rankers

terms.term: System A and System B learning
terms.definition: 06.2's split: System A learns by observation (extracting structure from passive sensory data); System B learns by acting toward goals; each is limited alone and the paper argues for integrating them so a system can learn and act continuously

The audio's name for Dreamer's compressed, low-dimensional code of the environment that keeps causal variables (where I am, where the diamond is) and drops visual noise; the paper itself says "representations" and "model state"

Audio terms for Dreamer parts: an encoder compresses the input to a latent state and a dynamics network predicts the next latent state from the current one and an action; the paper calls the latter the sequence model and dynamics predictor
A sequence of predicted states and actions run inside the world model without touching the real environment; Dreamer trains its actor and critic on such rollouts
The audio's term for models tied to real physical cause and effect, which text-only language models are said to lack; an idea from the world-model argument, not a measured property
The audio's examples of what an internal causal model must capture: objects stay where they are and actions have physical consequences; related to intuitive physics and object permanence in 06.3

A vendor memo's proposal (language, abstraction, memory, prediction, causality) for a hybrid composite intelligence; the memo is treated as a vendor document and the audio itself warns it advocates the company's own IP

The program summary's and audio's picture of future AI: language fluency plus perception, persistent memory, a world model and possibly symbolic reasoning, as modules, not one giant network; a hypothesis, not an established design
The scale-everything view: one ever-larger network will produce general intelligence; the argued-against position in the neurosymbolic paper and the vendor memo
How much text a model can read at once; the audio notes it is stateless working memory that is dropped when a session ends, so it does not give an agent lasting experience

The vendor memo's idea of a dedicated memory that filters, abstracts and consolidates experience into rules and updates them when contradicted; described only in the audio and a vendor document, so treat as a proposal
Audio phrase for an agent that keeps a continuing record of what it has learned across months of operation; vendor-memo language
Audio's term for governance and engineering that protects physical infrastructure when AI agents act on it, versus content filtering; from the vendor memo's argument
The audio's account of the memo: cryptographically signed agent actions, tamper-proof sandboxed memory and hard-coded non-differentiable limits on which systems an agent may touch

The audio's description of RLHF-style safety: a model learns to refuse recognizably dangerous requests, which the audio argues fails when an agent splits a goal into innocuous subtasks; this is the audio's argument and the memo's, not a finding in the report
An agent breaking a broad goal into many small steps that each look harmless, so request-level filters never trigger; an audio argument
How much harm a system can do; the audio says embodiment shifts it from informational risk to kinetic and cyber-physical risk

The audio's explanation that tiny per-step prediction errors multiply over long horizons; the GRASP source instead blames exploding or vanishing gradients, rough local minima and adversarial state gradients
Hard-coded constraints outside the learned network that a gradient-trained agent cannot optimize away; the vendor memo's safety idea as described in the audio
The audio claims an agent scoring 85% on SWE-bench drops to near zero in live repositories; no such figures appear in the R06 sources, which only say benchmarks overstate real-world utility
